scenes.animation: A school lab bench. A cartoon carbon atom with four outer electrons circling like fielders sits on a stool; Zippy tosses four extra electrons at it and they bounce off comically, then Zippy tries to yank four electrons away and the carbon atom holds on tight.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Carbon, just grab four more electrons and become C four minus. Noble gas configuration, done!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Nice try, Zippy. But carbon has only six protons. Holding on to ten electrons would be very difficult.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Fine. Then lose four electrons and become C four plus!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That would need a huge amount of energy to remove four electrons. So carbon does neither.

scenes.animation: A shell diagram builds up: nucleus labelled '6', K shell with 2 electrons, L shell with 4 electrons; the text 'Atomic number 6 → 2, 4' slides in and the four outer electrons glow yellow. Zippy appears holding a samosa split in half.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Carbon has atomic number six, so its electronic configuration is two, four. It needs four more electrons to reach a noble gas configuration.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Its solution is simple. It shares electrons.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Sharing? Like splitting a samosa with my best friend?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. A bond formed by sharing a pair of electrons between two atoms is called a covalent bond.

scenes.animation: Two hydrogen atoms drift together; their single electrons pair up as dots between them, then morph into one line 'H–H'. Next, two oxygen atoms share two pairs to form 'O=O', then two nitrogen atoms share three pairs to form 'N≡N', each with its electron dot structure beside it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons. That is a single bond, drawn as one line.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each oxygen atom has six valence electrons and needs two more. So two oxygen atoms share two pairs. That is a double bond.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And nitrogen has five and needs three. So a triple bond?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Correct. A nitrogen molecule has a triple bond.

scenes.animation: A carbon atom sits in the centre; four hydrogen atoms zoom in from four sides like fielders taking positions. Each shared pair appears as a dot-and-cross, then the picture switches to the structural formula of CH4 labelled 'Methane: four single covalent bonds'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now watch carbon in action. It shares its four valence electrons with four hydrogen atoms to form methane, C H four.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Methane is a major component of biogas and compressed natural gas, or CNG.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So is everyone in methane happy now?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Carbon now has eight electrons in its outer shell, and each hydrogen has two, like helium.

scenes.animation: A beaker of a covalent liquid boils over a small flame while a battery-and-bulb circuit dipped in it stays dark; label 'No ions → poor conductor'. Inside, molecules are held together by thick bonds but tug at each other with thin, weak strings. A yellow 'Board tip' sticky note flutters in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Covalent compounds have strong bonds within the molecule, but weak forces between molecules.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That is why most carbon compounds have low melting and boiling points. And since no ions are formed, they are poor conductors of electricity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: in electron dot structures, show only the outermost electrons, and count them before you finish.

scenes.animation: Neo stands beside a green chalkboard; three recap points tick in one by one: '1. Carbon (2, 4) cannot easily form C⁴⁻ or C⁴⁺', '2. It shares electrons: single, double, triple covalent bonds', '3. Covalent compounds: low m.p. and b.p., poor conductors'. Zippy high-fives the carbon atom.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Quick recap. One: carbon cannot easily gain or lose four electrons. Two: it shares electrons, forming single, double or triple covalent bonds. Three: covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Sharing is caring. Even for atoms!

scenes.animation: A towering heap of everyday items looms over Zippy: sugar packet, medicine strip, plastic toy, petrol can, cotton kurta, each stamped with a big 'C'. A counter in the corner spins up to 'about 3 million'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, why does everything in this pile have a big C stamped on it?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because they are all made of carbon compounds. The number of carbon compounds with known formulae was recently estimated at about three million.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Three million? From one little element?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two special properties explain it: catenation and tetravalency.

scenes.animation: Carbon atoms link hands to form a long straight chain, then a branch sprouts off the side, then the ends of another chain curl into a ring. The word 'Catenation' stamps across the screen in bold.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Catenation is carbon's unique ability to form bonds with other carbon atoms.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This gives rise to long chains, branched chains, and even carbon atoms arranged in rings.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can't any other element do that?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Silicon forms compounds with hydrogen having chains of only up to seven or eight atoms, and these compounds are very reactive. No other element shows catenation to the extent carbon does.

scenes.animation: A single carbon atom sprouts four arms; atoms wearing name tags 'O', 'H', 'N', 'S', 'Cl' and other carbons queue up to hold its hands, and the molecule reshuffles into a new compound each time a different atom joins.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Next, tetravalency. Carbon has a valency of four, so it can bond with four other atoms.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: These can be other carbon atoms, or atoms of oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many more.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each new partner gives a compound with different properties.

scenes.animation: Zoom into a tiny carbon nucleus gripping its shared electron pairs tightly, like a wicketkeeper holding a catch; beside it a big atom's nucleus fumbles its shared pair. Label: 'Small size → strong, stable bonds'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: But why are carbon's bonds so strong?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because carbon is small. Its nucleus holds the shared pairs of electrons strongly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So carbon compounds are exceptionally stable. Bonds formed by bigger atoms are much weaker.

scenes.animation: A board-exam answer sheet slides in with the question 'Give two reasons for the large number of carbon compounds.' Two neat bullet points write themselves: 'Catenation' and 'Tetravalency', each with a one-line explanation, and a red '2/2' appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: 'Why does carbon form so many compounds?' is a favourite two-mark question.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Write catenation and tetravalency, and explain each in one line. Mention the strong bonds due to small size for a complete answer.

scenes.animation: Chalkboard recap with three points ticking in: '1. Catenation: chains, branches, rings', '2. Tetravalency: bonds with 4 atoms', '3. Small size: strong, stable bonds'. Zippy flexes a tiny arm.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: catenation lets carbon form long chains, branched chains and rings. Two: tetravalency lets it bond with four atoms of carbon or other elements. Three: its small size makes these bonds strong and stable.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Small but mighty. Just like me!

scenes.animation: A cartoon 'Hydrocarbon Hostel'. In one room, carbon atoms each hold hands with one neighbour; in the next room, two carbon atoms hold hands twice. Zippy peeks through the door, puzzled.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, why are these two carbon atoms holding hands twice?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That is a double bond. Today we meet saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Hydrocarbons are compounds made of only carbon and hydrogen.

scenes.animation: Two carbon atoms join with a single line; six hydrogen atoms pop onto the free valencies, forming the structure of 'Ethane, C2H6'. A green stamp lands: 'Only single bonds = Saturated'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Take two carbon atoms joined by a single bond. Fill the remaining valencies with hydrogen, and you get ethane, C two H six.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Carbon compounds with only single bonds between carbon atoms are called saturated compounds.

scenes.animation: Two hydrogens are plucked off ethane and the carbons snap into a double bond: 'Ethene, C2H4'. Two more are plucked off and the bond becomes triple: 'Ethyne, C2H2'. Orange labels flash 'Unsaturated'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What if there aren't enough hydrogen atoms to go around?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then the carbon atoms satisfy their valency by forming double or triple bonds between themselves.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ethene, C two H four, has a double bond. Ethyne, C two H two, has a triple bond. These are unsaturated compounds.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Unsaturated carbon compounds are more reactive than saturated ones.

scenes.animation: Three columns slide in: 'Alkanes: CnH2n+2' with methane, 'Alkenes: CnH2n' with ethene, 'Alkynes: CnH2n−2' with ethyne. Each example builds itself atom by atom.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Saturated hydrocarbons are called alkanes, with the general formula C n H two n plus two.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Alkenes have one double bond, C n H two n. Alkynes have one triple bond, C n H two n minus two.

scenes.animation: Four carbon atoms line up straight as butane, then one hops to the side to form a branch; both versions show the same tag 'C4H10'. Then six carbons curl into cyclohexane, and a benzene ring with alternating double bonds spins in.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Do carbon chains always grow in a straight line?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. Butane, C four H ten, can have a straight chain or a branched chain. Same formula, different structures. These are structural isomers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Carbon atoms can even form rings, like cyclohexane, C six H twelve, and benzene, C six H six.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: after drawing any structure, check that every carbon has exactly four bonds. Examiners check that first.

scenes.animation: Chalkboard recap: '1. Saturated = only single bonds (alkanes)', '2. Unsaturated = double or triple bonds, more reactive', '3. Chains, branches, rings; isomers'. Zippy holds up scorecards reading 1, 2, 3.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: saturated hydrocarbons have only single bonds; they are alkanes. Two: unsaturated hydrocarbons have double or triple bonds and are more reactive. Three: carbon forms straight chains, branched chains and rings, and the same formula can have different structures.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Single, double, triple. Carbon is basically a cricket scoreboard!

scenes.animation: A family photo on a living-room wall: Methane, Ethane, Propane and Butane stand in height order like siblings, each one a '–CH2–' block taller. Zippy measures them with a ruler.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: These molecules look like siblings lined up for a family photo!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Good eye. They belong to a homologous series.

scenes.animation: CH3OH, C2H5OH, C3H7OH and C4H9OH stack up; a glowing '–CH2–' block slides in between each pair with a bouncing label '+14 u'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A homologous series is a series of compounds in which the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen in a carbon chain.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Look at C H three O H, C two H five O H, C three H seven O H. Each member differs from the next by a C H two unit.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the mass goes up by fourteen every time?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. One carbon of twelve u plus two hydrogens gives fourteen u.

scenes.animation: A bar graph of boiling points climbs like a staircase along the series, while each member wears the same badge 'Same chemical properties'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: As molecular mass increases, physical properties like melting point, boiling point and solubility show a gradation.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But chemical properties stay similar, because they are decided by the functional group.

scenes.animation: A carbon chain tries on different hats, each lighting up with its name: '–Cl / –Br: Halo', '–OH: Alcohol', '–CHO: Aldehyde', '–CO–: Ketone', '–COOH: Carboxylic acid'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Functional group? Like a class WhatsApp group?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not quite. Heteroatoms like oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur or a halogen replace hydrogen in a hydrocarbon chain.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The heteroatom, or the group containing it, gives the compound its specific properties. That is the functional group.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Halo group is chlorine or bromine. Alcohol is O H. Aldehyde is C H O. Ketone is a C double bond O within the chain. Carboxylic acid is C O O H.

scenes.animation: A board-exam question card: 'Write the next homologue of CH3OH.' Zippy scribbles 'C2H4OH', a buzzer sounds and it gets a red cross; Neo writes 'C2H5OH' with a green tick.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next homologue of methanol? Easy, C two H four O H!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Close, but no. Add a full C H two unit. The answer is C two H five O H, ethanol.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: always add C H two, never just a carbon. Then check that each carbon has four bonds.

scenes.animation: Chalkboard recap: '1. Same functional group; members differ by CH2 (14 u)', '2. Physical properties: gradation; chemical properties: similar', '3. Functional groups: –X, –OH, –CHO, –CO–, –COOH'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: members of a homologous series have the same functional group and differ by C H two, that is fourteen u. Two: physical properties show gradation, chemical properties stay similar. Three: functional groups like O H, C H O, C O and C O O H decide chemical behaviour.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Family traits, but with chemistry!

scenes.animation: A molecule stands at a school admission desk; the clerk, a talking test tube wearing spectacles, holds a register and asks for its name. The molecule shrugs; Zippy bounces in shouting names.

lines.speaker: TEST TUBE
lines.text: Name, please? I cannot admit a molecule without a proper name.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Let's call it Bunty!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Chemists prefer a system, Zippy. Let's name it the IUPAC way, in three steps.

scenes.animation: The molecule's carbon chain lights up atom by atom as it is counted; a table slides in: '1 C: meth', '2 C: eth', '3 C: prop', '4 C: but', '5 C: pent', '6 C: hex'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step one: count the carbon atoms in the chain. One carbon is meth, two is eth, three is prop, four is but, five is pent, six is hex.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So a three-carbon chain gets the parent name propane.

scenes.animation: Functional group cards flip over one by one: 'Chloro- / Bromo- (prefix)', '-ol (alcohol)', '-al (aldehyde)', '-one (ketone)', '-oic acid (carboxylic acid)', '-ene (double bond)', '-yne (triple bond)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step two: identify the functional group. It is shown as either a prefix or a suffix.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Halogens become prefixes, like chloro or bromo. Alcohol is ol, aldehyde is al, ketone is one, and carboxylic acid is oic acid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A double bond is ene, and a triple bond is yne. So a three-carbon chain with a double bond is propene.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And a two-carbon chain with a triple bond is ethyne?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Spot on.

scenes.animation: The final 'e' of 'propane' is rubbed off with a pencil eraser as '-one' snaps in to make 'propanone'. A table fills in: 'CH3CH2CH2Cl → chloropropane', 'CH3CH2CHO → propanal', 'CH3COCH3 → propanone', 'CH3CH2COOH → propanoic acid'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step three: if the suffix begins with a vowel, drop the final e of the parent name. Propane plus one becomes propanone.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So a three-carbon aldehyde is propanal?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. A three-carbon acid is propanoic acid. And with chlorine as a prefix, it is chloropropane.

scenes.animation: Zippy proudly writes 'CH3CHO = methanal' on the board; a buzzer sounds and Neo circles both carbon atoms in red, then rewrites it as 'ethanal' with a tick. A 'Board tip' sticky note appears.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Easy one! C H three C H O has one C H three, so it's methanal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Careful. The carbon in C H O also counts. That's two carbons, so it is ethanal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: always count the carbon inside the functional group. It is the most common naming mistake.

scenes.animation: Chalkboard recap: '1. Count carbons: meth, eth, prop, but', '2. Add prefix or suffix for the functional group', '3. Drop final e before a vowel suffix'. The test tube clerk stamps 'ADMITTED' on the register.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: count the carbon atoms to get the parent name. Two: add the functional group as a prefix or a suffix. Three: drop the final e before a suffix that starts with a vowel.

lines.speaker: TEST TUBE
lines.text: Propanone. Admitted!

scenes.animation: A home kitchen: a steel pan on the gas stove has a sooty black bottom, the burner shows a lazy yellow flame, and Zippy pops up from behind it with a soot-covered face.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, the gas stove turned this pan black. And my face!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A yellow, sooty flame means the fuel isn't burning completely. The air holes are probably blocked.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Let's look at four reactions of carbon compounds: combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution.

scenes.animation: Equations write themselves in flame: 'C + O2 → CO2 + heat and light' and 'CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O + heat and light'. Split screen: a clean blue flame labelled 'Saturated' and a yellow smoky flame labelled 'Unsaturated'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Combustion: carbon and its compounds burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide, along with heat and light.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Methane burns as C H four plus two O two gives C O two plus two H two O.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Saturated hydrocarbons generally give a clean blue flame. Unsaturated ones give a yellow flame with lots of black smoke.

scenes.animation: A drop of purple 'alkaline KMnO4' falls into warm ethanol and the purple colour fades; an arrow shows 'CH3CH2OH → CH3COOH', and the KMnO4 bottle wears a cape labelled 'Oxidising agent'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Oxidation: alcohols can be converted to carboxylic acids by oxidising agents like alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So ethanol becomes ethanoic acid. An oxidising agent is a substance that adds oxygen to others.

scenes.animation: A vegetable oil bottle; H2 molecules rush in escorted by a nickel coin labelled 'Catalyst'. The double bonds in the oil molecules open up and each carbon grabs a hydrogen, turning the oil into a solid fat.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Addition: unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of catalysts like palladium or nickel, giving saturated compounds.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This is used in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So which is healthier, oil or animal fat?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Oils with unsaturated fatty acids are better. Animal fats contain saturated fatty acids, which are said to be harmful for health.

scenes.animation: A methane molecule sunbathes on a beach chair; a chlorine atom swaps places with one hydrogen, which walks off holding the other chlorine. Equation: 'CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl' with 'sunlight' written over the arrow.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Substitution: saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive. But in sunlight, chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms one by one.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: C H four plus C l two, in the presence of sunlight, gives C H three C l plus H C l.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: always write the condition over the arrow. Sunlight for substitution, nickel or palladium catalyst for addition.

scenes.animation: Chalkboard recap: '1. Combustion: CO2 + heat + light', '2. Oxidation: ethanol → ethanoic acid; Addition: H2 + Ni/Pd', '3. Substitution: Cl replaces H in sunlight'. Zippy scrubs the stove burner clean.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: combustion gives carbon dioxide, heat and light, and saturated fuels burn with a clean blue flame. Two: oxidising agents turn ethanol into ethanoic acid, and hydrogen adds to unsaturated compounds with a catalyst. Three: in sunlight, chlorine substitutes hydrogen in methane.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And I'll unblock the stove's air holes!

scenes.animation: A kitchen shelf: a jar of Nani's mango pickle and a cough syrup bottle chat like neighbours. Zippy sniffs each one and pulls a face.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why does Nani's pickle smell sour, and this cough syrup smell like a hospital?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Meet two famous carbon compounds: ethanoic acid in vinegar, and ethanol in the syrup.

scenes.animation: An ethanol character in a 'C2H5OH' T-shirt; a small piece of sodium drops into it and bubbles fizz; a lit splinter makes a 'pop'. Equation: '2Na + 2CH3CH2OH → 2CH3CH2O⁻Na⁺ + H2'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ethanol is a liquid at room temperature and mixes with water in all proportions. It is used in tincture of iodine, cough syrups and tonics.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Even a small amount of pure ethanol, called absolute alcohol, can be lethal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ethanol reacts with sodium to give sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas.

scenes.animation: Ethanol is heated at '443 K' with excess 'conc. H2SO4'; a water droplet is yanked out of the molecule and it becomes 'CH2=CH2 (ethene) + H2O'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Heat ethanol at four hundred forty-three kelvin with excess concentrated sulphuric acid, and it loses water to give ethene.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Here, concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent.

scenes.animation: A vinegar bottle labelled '5–8% ethanoic acid in water'. Cut to a snowy hill station where a bottle of pure ethanoic acid freezes into icy crystals: 'Glacial acetic acid, m.p. 290 K'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ethanoic acid, also called acetic acid, is a weak acid. A five to eight percent solution in water is vinegar, used to preserve pickles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pure ethanoic acid melts at two hundred ninety kelvin, so it often freezes in cold climates. That's why it's called glacial acetic acid.

scenes.animation: Ethanol and ethanoic acid shake hands over a drop of acid catalyst; a flower-scented cloud floats up: 'CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH → CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O'. Then a baking-soda packet fizzes in vinegar: 'CH3COOH + NaHCO3 → CH3COONa + H2O + CO2'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol, with an acid catalyst, to form an ester. Esters are sweet-smelling and used in perfumes and flavouring agents.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Treat the ester with sodium hydroxide, and you get back the alcohol and sodium ethanoate. This is saponification.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: With carbonates and hydrogencarbonates, ethanoic acid gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Like baking soda fizzing in vinegar!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: to tell ethanol from ethanoic acid, add sodium hydrogencarbonate. Only the acid gives brisk bubbles of carbon dioxide.

scenes.animation: Chalkboard recap: '1. Ethanol + Na → H2; + hot conc. H2SO4 → ethene', '2. Ethanoic acid: weak acid; vinegar = 5–8%', '3. Acid + alcohol → ester; acid + carbonate → CO2'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: ethanol gives hydrogen with sodium, and ethene with hot concentrated sulphuric acid. Two: ethanoic acid is a weak acid, and vinegar is its five to eight percent solution. Three: acid plus alcohol gives a sweet-smelling ester, and acid plus a carbonate gives carbon dioxide.

scenes.animation: Zippy splashes curry on a white school shirt; he scrubs it under plain tap water and the yellow oil stain just slides around, grinning back at him.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Water isn't working! This curry stain is laughing at me!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Oil and water don't mix, Zippy. You need soap. Let's see why it works.

scenes.animation: A soap molecule appears as a tadpole: a round red head labelled 'Ionic end: hydrophilic' and a long wavy tail labelled 'Hydrocarbon chain: hydrophobic'. The head splashes happily in water; the tail dives into an oil drop.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A soap molecule has two ends. The ionic end interacts with water, so it is hydrophilic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The long carbon chain avoids water and dissolves in oil. It is hydrophobic.

scenes.animation: Hundreds of tadpole molecules surround the oil droplet with tails pointing inward into the oil and heads facing outward into the water, forming a ball labelled 'Micelle'. Rinse water carries the balls away, and the shirt gleams white.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In water, soap molecules cluster so that the tails are inside, away from water, and the ionic ends face outward. This cluster is a micelle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The oily dirt collects in the centre of the micelle, and rinsing washes it away.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why don't the micelles clump together again?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because of ion-ion repulsion. They stay in the solution as a colloid.

scenes.animation: Scene shifts to a handpump bucket labelled 'Hard water: Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺'. Soap is added, and instead of lather, a white curdy layer labelled 'Scum' floats up. Zippy scrubs harder and gets nowhere.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now try soap in hard water. Calcium and magnesium salts react with soap to form an insoluble substance called scum.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A lot of soap is wasted, and very little lather forms.

scenes.animation: A detergent molecule jumps in wearing a badge 'Sulphonate / Ammonium salt'; in the same hard-water bucket it lathers happily and bubbles rise. A 'Board tip' card shows a micelle with a red circle around the inward-pointing tails.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Detergents solve this. They are generally sodium salts of sulphonic acids, or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Their charged ends do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so they work even in hard water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's why detergents are used in shampoos and for washing clothes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: when you draw a micelle, point the tails inward into the oil. Reversed tails is the most common mistake.

scenes.animation: Chalkboard recap: '1. Soap: hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tail', '2. Micelle traps oily dirt in the centre', '3. Hard water → scum; detergents still lather'. Zippy holds up the spotless shirt.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: soap molecules have a hydrophilic ionic end and a hydrophobic carbon chain. Two: they form micelles that trap oily dirt in the centre. Three: soaps form scum in hard water, but detergents keep working.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Shirt saved. Mission accomplished!
